claim: Mitochondria display dynamic subcellular distribution in alveolar epithelial cells during alveolar formation.
source: We found that mitochondria were widely distributed in alveolar epithelial cells (distinguished by T1α and SPC for AT1 and AT2 cells, respectively) and myofibroblasts (marked by PDGF receptor A [PDGFRA] and smooth muscle actin [SMA]) (Sun et al., 2000; Gouveia et al., 2017; Figure 1A). This is consistent with an essential role of mitochondrial activity in proper functioning of lung cells. In addition, we observed an uneven subcellular distribution of mitochondria (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing MPC1 and MTCO1 distribution in lung sections (Figure 1A) and transmission electron microscopy (Figure 1B).

claim: Mitochondria were concentrated in areas adjacent to the trans-Golgi network in alveolar epithelial cells, especially AT1 cells.
source: For instance, mitochondria were concentrated in areas adjacent to the trans-Golgi network (TGN38+) in alveolar epithelial cells (especially AT1 cells) where proteins were sorted to reach their destinations through vesicles and in areas that surrounded SMA in myofibroblasts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing colocalization of mitochondrial markers with TGN38 in Figure 1A.

claim: Mitochondria were concentrated in areas that surrounded smooth muscle actin in myofibroblasts.
source: For instance, mitochondria were concentrated in areas adjacent to the trans-Golgi network (TGN38+) in alveolar epithelial cells (especially AT1 cells) where proteins were sorted to reach their destinations through vesicles and in areas that surrounded SMA in myofibroblasts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and electron microscopy data in Figure 1A and B showing mitochondrial distribution around SMA in myofibroblasts.

claim: Localized mitochondrial distribution is required for cellular function in mammalian lungs.
source: This finding suggests that localized mitochondrial distribution is required for cellular function in mammalian lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of uneven subcellular distribution of mitochondria in specific functional locations.

claim: Compromised mitochondrial activity in the postnatal murine lung leads to defective alveologenesis.
source: We noticed that multiple regions in the lungs of mutant mice displayed alveolar defects concomitant with an increased mean linear intercept (MLI), a measure of air space size (Campbell and Tomkeieff, 1952; Escolar et al., 1994; Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and MLI measurements in Tfamf/f; CAGGCreER/+ mice showing enlarged saccules and increased MLI (Figure 2C and D).

claim: Alveolar defects in Tfamf/f; CAGGCreER/+ mice were associated with disorganized smooth muscle actin.
source: Alveolar defects were associated with disorganized SMA (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing disorganized SMA in Figure 2E.

claim: The relative ratio of mitochondrial DNA to nuclear DNA was reduced in Tfam-deficient lungs compared to controls.
source: Indeed, the relative ratio of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) (Venegas and Halberg, 2012), 16S rRNA, and mitochondrially encoded NADH dehydrogenase 1 (mtND1), to nuclear DNA (nDNA), hexokinase 2 (Hk2), was reduced in Tfam-deficient lungs compared to controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis showing reduced mtDNA/nDNA ratio in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of Tfam was accompanied by diminished immunoreactivity of MTCO1.
source: Loss of Tfam was accompanied by diminished immunoreactivity of MTCO1, the expression of which is controlled by Tfam (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2G showing reduced MTCO1 signal.

claim: Mitochondrial activity is required for alveolar formation.
source: Together, these results indicate that mitochondrial activity is required for alveolar formation.
evidence: Inferred from the alveolar defects observed when mitochondrial activity is compromised through Tfam deletion.

claim: Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency.
source: Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency and could not be distinguished from their wild-type littermates by their outer appearance at birth.
evidence: Observation of mouse breeding outcomes.

claim: Branching morphogenesis and saccule formation were unaffected by inactivating Tfam in SOX9+ cells.
source: Moreover, histological analysis revealed no difference between control and mutant lungs prior to P5, confirming that branching morphogenesis and saccule formation were unaffected by inactivating Tfam in SOX9+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis showing normal lung structure at P0 in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Differentiation of alveolar type I and type II cells proceeded normally in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: In addition, differentiation of alveolar type I and type II cells proceeded normally in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing normal expression of cell type markers in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: These results highlight a difference in dependence on mitochondrial activity in distinct cellular processes during development.
source: These results highlight a difference in dependence on mitochondrial activity in distinct cellular processes during development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some developmental processes (branching, sacculation, cell differentiation) are unaffected while alveolar formation is impaired.

claim: Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice could be discerned by their slightly reduced body size after P5.
source: After P5, Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice could be discerned by their slightly reduced body size in comparison with the littermate controls.
evidence: Observation of mouse phenotypes.

claim: Histological analysis of Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs at various postnatal stages revealed defects in secondary septa formation with an increased MLI.
source: Histological analysis of Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs at various postnatal stages revealed defects in secondary septa formation with an increased MLI (Figure 3A and B) and reduced primary septal thickness (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by histological images and MLI measurements in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Primary septal thickness appears to be an earlier and more sensitive indicator than MLI in detecting defects in secondary septation.
source: In this setting, primary septal thickness (P2–P7) appears to be an earlier and more sensitive indicator than MLI in detecting defects in secondary septation.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal pattern of changes in primary septal thickness versus MLI measurements.

claim: No apparent difference in cell death was noted between control and Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: No apparent difference in cell death was noted between control and Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that mitochondria-mediated apoptosis was not activated.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Mitochondria-mediated apoptosis was not activated in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: No apparent difference in cell death was noted between control and Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that mitochondria-mediated apoptosis was not activated.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increased cell death despite mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 3D), mitochondrial complex I activity (Figure 3E) and ATP production (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3D.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed reduced mitochondrial complex I activity.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 3D), mitochondrial complex I activity (Figure 3E) and ATP production (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data in Figure 3E.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed reduced ATP production.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 3D), mitochondrial complex I activity (Figure 3E) and ATP production (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by ATP measurement data in Figure 3F.

claim: Loss of epithelial Tfam did not affect the major regulators of mitochondrial fusion and fission such as OPA1 processing and DRP1 phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, loss of epithelial Tfam did not affect the major regulators of mitochondrial fusion and fission such as OPA1 processing and DRP1 phosphorylation (Chan, 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: These findings are consistent with reduced mitochondrial activity in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs and reveal a critical role of mitochondrial activity in lung epithelial cells during alveologenesis.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with reduced mitochondrial activity in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs and reveal a critical role of mitochondrial activity in lung epithelial cells during alveologenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced mitochondrial function and alveolar defects.

claim: Removal of Tfam in T cells by Foxp3-Cre or Cd4-Cre did not exhibit alveolar defects.
source: We noted that removal of Tfam in T cells by Foxp3-Cre (Rubtsov et al., 2008) or Cd4-Cre (Lee et al., 2001) and in macrophages by activated Cx3cr1-CreER (Yona et al., 2013) did not exhibit alveolar defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Fu et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and cited studies.

claim: Removal of Tfam in macrophages by activated Cx3cr1-CreER did not exhibit alveolar defects.
source: We noted that removal of Tfam in T cells by Foxp3-Cre (Rubtsov et al., 2008) or Cd4-Cre (Lee et al., 2001) and in macrophages by activated Cx3cr1-CreER (Yona et al., 2013) did not exhibit alveolar defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Fu et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and cited studies.

claim: Structural components of the secondary septa are more susceptible to reduced mitochondrial function than T cells and macrophages.
source: This suggests that structural components of the secondary septa are more susceptible to reduced mitochondrial function.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of Tfam deletion in different cell types.

claim: Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency.
source: Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency and cannot be distinguished from their wild-type littermates by their outer appearance or activity at birth.
evidence: Observation of mouse breeding outcomes.

claim: No difference between control and Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs prior to P5 was detected by histological analysis.
source: Similarly, no difference between control and mutant lungs prior to P5 was detected by histological analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice displayed defects in secondary septation after P5.
source: After P5, Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice displayed defects in secondary septation (Figure 3G) with an increased MLI (Figure 3H) and reduced primary septal thickness (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and measurements in Figure 3G, H, and I.

claim: Loss of epithelial Rhot1 did not induce cell death.
source: Loss of epithelial Rhot1 did not induce cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mitochondrial activity was unperturbed by disrupting epithelial Rhot1.
source: As expected, mitochondrial activity was unperturbed by disrupting epithelial Rhot1. No changes in mtDNA/nDNA ratio, mitochondrial complex I activity, or ATP production were observed in lysates from Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 3J–L).
evidence: Supported by qPCR, enzymatic activity, and ATP measurement data in Figure 3J-L.

claim: Localized mitochondrial distribution plays a functional role in alveolar formation.
source: These results support the notion that localized mitochondrial distribution plays a functional role in alveolar formation.
evidence: Inferred from the alveolar defects observed when mitochondrial distribution is disrupted through Rhot1 deletion.

claim: The alveolar defects in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs were less severe than those in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: We noticed that the alveolar defects in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs were less severe than those in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Comparative observation of phenotype severity between the two mutant lines.

claim: The less severe phenotype in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs is likely due to the fact that only the distribution and not the activity of mitochondria was perturbed.
source: This is likely due to the fact that only the distribution and not the activity of mitochondria was perturbed in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on mitochondrial function between Tfam and Rhot1 deletion.

claim: The number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts marked by PDGFRA was reduced in the absence of epithelial Tfam.
source: Interestingly, the number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts marked by PDGFRA was reduced in the absence of epithelial Tfam (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 4A and D.

claim: The number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was reduced in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs where epithelial Rhot1 was lost.
source: Likewise, we found that the number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was reduced in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs where epithelial Rhot1 was lost (Figure 4G and I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 4G and I.

claim: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA, indicative of PDGF signaling, was reduced in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA (p-PDGFRA), indicative of PDGF signaling, was reduced in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 4A and G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4A.

claim: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA was reduced in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Phosphorylation of PDGFRA (p-PDGFRA), indicative of PDGF signaling, was reduced in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs (Figure 4A and G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4G.

claim: PDGF signal reception by fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was impaired in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: This observation suggests that PDGF signal reception by fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was impaired in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced phosphorylation of PDGFRA.

claim: PDGF signal reception by fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was impaired in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: This observation suggests that PDGF signal reception by fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was impaired in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced phosphorylation of PDGFRA.

claim: Production of the PDGF ligand (PDGFA) in alveolar epithelial cells was unaffected in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by qPCR analysis.
source: We found that production of the PDGF ligand (PDGFA) in alveolar epithelial cells was unaffected in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by qPCR analysis (Figure 4E and J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4E.

claim: Production of the PDGF ligand (PDGFA) in alveolar epithelial cells was unaffected in Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by qPCR analysis.
source: We found that production of the PDGF ligand (PDGFA) in alveolar epithelial cells was unaffected in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ or Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs by qPCR analysis (Figure 4E and J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4J.

claim: LacZ expression in Pdgfa-expressing cells displayed a similar pattern and intensity between control and Tfam-deficient lungs.
source: We found that LacZ expression in Pdgfa-expressing cells (i.e., alveolar epithelial cells) displayed a similar pattern and intensity between control and Tfam-deficient lungs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by LacZ staining data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: These results pointed to disrupted PDGF trafficking or release in Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
source: Together, these results pointed to disrupted PDGF trafficking or release. This defect would subsequently disturb signal reception in mesenchymal fibroblasts/myofibroblasts of Tfamf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Rhot1f/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Inferred from normal PDGF production but impaired signaling.

claim: PDGF levels in the conditioned media derived from Tfam-deficient cells were reduced compared to controls.
source: PDGF levels in the conditioned media derived from Tfam- or Rhot1-deficient cells were reduced compared to controls (Figure 4F and K).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of supernatants in Figure 4F.

claim: PDGF levels in the conditioned media derived from Rhot1-deficient cells were reduced compared to controls.
source: PDGF levels in the conditioned media derived from Tfam- or Rhot1-deficient cells were reduced compared to controls (Figure 4F and K).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of supernatants in Figure 4K.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial activity results in a failure of vesicular transport and PDGF release from alveolar epithelial cells.
source: These findings support a model in which loss of mitochondrial activity or distribution results in a failure of vesicular transport and PDGF release from alveolar epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced PDGF secretion in Tfam-deficient cells.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial distribution results in a failure of vesicular transport and PDGF release from alveolar epithelial cells.
source: These findings support a model in which loss of mitochondrial activity or distribution results in a failure of vesicular transport and PDGF release from alveolar epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced PDGF secretion in Rhot1-deficient cells.

claim: These defects are in part due to an incapacitated actomyosin cytoskeleton caused by reduced mitochondrial function.
source: We surmise that these defects are in part due to an incapacitated actomyosin cytoskeleton caused by reduced mitochondrial function.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the known role of the actomyosin cytoskeleton in vesicular transport.

claim: Approximately 95% of PDGFRA+ lineaged cells are myofibroblasts.
source: It was reported that ~95% of lineaged cells (PDGFRA+) are myofibroblasts (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Li et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of Tfam in the lung mesenchyme did not affect branching morphogenesis or saccule formation.
source: This suggests that loss of Tfam in the lung mesenchyme did not affect branching morphogenesis or saccule formation (Metzger et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of phenotypic differences prior to P3 and cited reference.

claim: Histological analysis of Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs at various postnatal stages prior to P5 revealed defective secondary septa formation with an increased MLI.
source: Histological analysis of Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs at various postnatal stages prior to P5 revealed defective secondary septa formation with an increased MLI (Figure 5A and B) and reduced primary septal thickness (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by histological images and measurements in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: Loss of mesenchymal Tfam did not induce cell death.
source: Loss of mesenchymal Tfam did not induce cell death (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 5D), mitochondrial complex I/IV activity (Figure 5E), and ATP production (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 5D.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed reduced mitochondrial complex I/IV activity.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 5D), mitochondrial complex I/IV activity (Figure 5E), and ATP production (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assay data in Figure 5E.

claim: Lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed reduced ATP production.
source: Moreover, lysates from Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a reduction in mtDNA/nDNA ratio (Figure 5D), mitochondrial complex I/IV activity (Figure 5E), and ATP production (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by ATP measurement data in Figure 5F.

claim: All findings are consistent with reduced mitochondrial activity in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs.
source: All of them are consistent with reduced mitochondrial activity in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced mtDNA, complex activity, and ATP production.

claim: Most Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice died before P30.
source: Most Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice died before P30.
evidence: Observation of mouse survival.

claim: Tfamf/f; Twist2Cre/+ mice exhibited alveolar defects similar to those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice.
source: Tfamf/f; Twist2Cre/+ mice exhibited alveolar defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B) similar to those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice, further supporting a central role of mitochondrial activity in the lung mesenchyme during alveologenesis.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and MLI measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Lrpprcf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice developed alveolar defects.
source: We found that Lrpprcf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice developed alveolar defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D), albeit the phenotypes were less severe than those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and MLI measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: The phenotypes in Lrpprcf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice were less severe than those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice, likely due to the presence of residual proteins after removal of Lrpprc.
source: This was likely due to the presence of residual proteins after removal of Lrpprc.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying phenotype severity differences.

claim: These studies establish a crucial role of mitochondrial activity in fibroblasts/myofibroblasts for alveologenesis.
source: Together, these studies establish a crucial role of mitochondrial activity in fibroblasts/myofibroblasts for alveologenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the alveolar defects observed when mitochondrial activity is disrupted in mesenchymal cells.

claim: Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice exhibited alveolar defects, milder than those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs.
source: Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice exhibited alveolar defects (Figure 5G–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), milder than those in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and measurements in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Mitochondrial activity was unperturbed by disrupting mesenchymal Rhot1.
source: Mitochondrial activity was unperturbed by disrupting mesenchymal Rhot1 (Figure 5J–L).
evidence: Supported by qPCR, enzymatic activity, and ATP measurement data in Figure 5J-L.

claim: Fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation was reduced in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs compared to controls.
source: We discovered that fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation was reduced in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ or Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs compared to controls (Figure 6A, B, E and F), suggesting defective PDGF signal reception.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation was reduced in Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs compared to controls.
source: We discovered that fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation was reduced in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ or Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs compared to controls (Figure 6A, B, E and F), suggesting defective PDGF signal reception.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Reduced fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation suggests defective PDGF signal reception.
source: We discovered that fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation was reduced in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ or Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs compared to controls (Figure 6A, B, E and F), suggesting defective PDGF signal reception.
evidence: Inferred from the known role of PDGF signaling in fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation.

claim: Defective PDGF signal reception may be related to a failure in PDGFR trafficking when mitochondrial function is impaired.
source: This may be related to a failure in PDGFR trafficking when mitochondrial function is impaired.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying defective PDGF signaling.

claim: The pool of PDGFRA+ myofibroblasts was decreased with a concomitant reduction in SMA and/or elastin, contributing to alveolar defects.
source: As a result, the pool of PDGFRA+ myofibroblasts was decreased with a concomitant reduction in SMA (encoded by Acta2) and/or elastin (Figure 6C and G), contributing to alveolar defects.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing reduced expression of Acta2 and Eln in Figure 6C and G.

claim: Proper activity and distribution of mitochondria in alveolar fibroblasts/myofibroblasts are critical to generating a sufficient number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts for secondary septation.
source: In summary, these findings suggest that proper activity and distribution of mitochondria in alveolar fibroblasts/myofibroblasts are critical to generating a sufficient number of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts for secondary septation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced fibroblast/myofibroblast numbers and alveolar defects.

claim: Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts displayed short tubular and fragmented mitochondria.
source: Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts displayed short tubular and fragmented mitochondria (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Only scant Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts were detected in the cell-free area after 36-48 hours in wound healing assays.
source: While control fibroblasts/myofibroblasts occupied the cell-free area after 36–48 hr, only scant Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts were detected in the cell-free area (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data in Figure 6D.

claim: Introduction of TFAM into Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts rescued their migratory defects.
source: Introduction of TFAM into Tfam-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts rescued their migratory defects (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, and E).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, and E.

claim: Mobility of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was compromised due to loss of mitochondrial activity in these cells.
source: This result indicates that mobility of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts was compromised due to loss of mitochondrial activity in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from the wound healing assay results showing reduced migration.

claim: The migration defect was in part due to an incapacitated actomyosin cytoskeleton without mitochondrial activity.
source: We conjecture that the migration defect was in part due to an incapacitated actomyosin cytoskeleton without mitochondrial activity.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the known role of the actomyosin cytoskeleton in cell migration.

claim: Organization of the cytoskeleton was perturbed in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs in comparison with controls.
source: Consistent with this idea, organization of the cytoskeleton (labeled by phalloidin) was perturbed in Tfamf/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs in comparison with controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data in Figure 6A.

claim: Fibroblasts/myofibroblasts derived from Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a compromised response in wound healing assays compared to controls.
source: Similarly, fibroblasts/myofibroblasts derived from Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a compromised response in wound healing assays compared to controls (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D), which was restored by RHOT1 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data in Figure 6H.

claim: Migration defects in Rhot1-deficient fibroblasts/myofibroblasts were restored by RHOT1 expression.
source: Similarly, fibroblasts/myofibroblasts derived from Rhot1f/f; PdgfraCre/+ lungs displayed a compromised response in wound healing assays compared to controls (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D), which was restored by RHOT1 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: These results affirm the role of mitochondrial activity and distribution in regulating fibroblasts/myofibroblasts contraction and/or migration during alveologenesis.
source: To sum up, these results affirm the role of mitochondrial activity and distribution in regulating fibroblasts/myofibroblasts contraction and/or migration during alveologenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of migration defects and their rescue.

claim: Rptorf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice failed to survive to term.
source: Rptorf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Rptorf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice failed to survive to term, precluding the analysis of potential alveolar phenotypes.
evidence: Observation of mouse survival.

claim: Rptorf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice failed to survive to term.
source: Rptorf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Rptorf/f; PdgfraCre/+ mice failed to survive to term, precluding the analysis of potential alveolar phenotypes.
evidence: Observation of mouse survival.

claim: Analysis of Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ mice at P10 revealed alveolar defects with an increased MLI.
source: Analysis of Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ mice at P10 revealed alveolar defects with an increased MLI (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and MLI measurements in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Defective secondary septation in Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ lungs was associated with reduced SMA.
source: Defective secondary septation in Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ lungs was associated with reduced SMA (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7D.

claim: The protein levels of phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (p-RPS6) were decreased in lysates from Rptor-deficient lungs compared to controls.
source: As expected, the protein levels of phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (p-RPS6), a downstream target of mTORC1, were decreased in lysates from Rptor-deficient lungs compared to controls (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relative ratio of mtDNA to nDNA was reduced in Rptor-deficient lungs.
source: The relative ratio of mtDNA to nDNA was reduced in Rptor-deficient lungs (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 7F.

claim: Immunoreactivity of both MPC1 and MTCO1 was diminished in Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ lungs compared to controls.
source: Moreover, immunoreactivity of both MPC1 and MTCO1 was diminished in Rptorf/f; CAGGCreER/+ lungs compared to controls (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7G.

claim: Elimination of Rptor in the lung resulted in loss of mitochondria.
source: These findings show that elimination of Rptor in the lung resulted in loss of mitochondria.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced mtDNA and mitochondrial protein expression.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial function contributed to alveolar defects in Rptor-deficient lungs.
source: Impaired mitochondrial function then contributed to alveolar defects.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between reduced mitochondrial function and alveolar defects.

claim: mTORC1 controls alveolar formation partly through its effects on mitochondrial function.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that mTORC1 controls alveolar formation partly through its effects on mitochondrial function.
evidence: Inferred from the alveolar defects and reduced mitochondrial function in Rptor-deficient lungs.

claim: The copy number of mitochondria relative to nuclear DNA was significantly reduced in COPD/emphysema patients.
source: We found that the copy number of mitochondria (Venegas and Halberg, 2012) relative to nuclear DNA was significantly reduced in COPD/emphysema patients (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from human lung samples in Figure 8B.

claim: TFAM protein levels were reduced in lysates from emphysema lungs compared to normal lungs.
source: In addition, TFAM protein levels were reduced in lysates from emphysema lungs compared to normal lungs (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung samples in Figure 8C.

claim: These results established a connection between mitochondrial function and pathogenesis of COPD/emphysema.
source: These results established a connection between mitochondrial function and pathogenesis of COPD/emphysema.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced mitochondrial copy number and TFAM levels in emphysema patients.

claim: A disorganized cytoskeleton was noted in COPD/emphysema lungs, in which actin bundles seen in normal alveoli were sparse.
source: Interestingly, a disorganized cytoskeleton was noted in COPD/emphysema lungs, in which actin bundles seen in normal alveoli were sparse (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data from human lung samples in Figure 8D.

claim: No difference in the protein levels of either RPS6 or p-RPS6 was detected in lysates from emphysema and normal lungs.
source: We did not detect a difference in the protein levels of either RPS6 or p-RPS6 in lysates from emphysema and normal lungs (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung samples in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heterogeneous expression of p-RPS6 was observed in emphysema lungs.
source: However, we observed heterogeneous expression of p-RPS6 in emphysema lungs.
evidence: Observation from immunostaining data.

claim: The amount of PDGFA released into the media was reduced in TFAM-knockdown human lung epithelial cells compared to controls.
source: The amount of PDGFA released into the media was reduced in TFAM-knockdown cells compared to controls and was rescued by expression of mTFAMFLAG (n = 3 for each group).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung epithelial cells in Figure 8F.

claim: PDGFA secretion defect in TFAM-knockdown human lung epithelial cells was rescued by expression of mouse TFAM.
source: The amount of PDGFA released into the media was reduced in TFAM-knockdown cells compared to controls and was rescued by expression of mTFAMFLAG (n = 3 for each group).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung epithelial cells in Figure 8F.

claim: The migratory defect of TFAM-knockdown human lung fibroblasts was rescued by mouse TFAM expression.
source: The migratory defect of fibroblasts was rescued by mTFAMFLAG expression (n = 3 for each group).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data from human lung fibroblasts in Figure 8G.

claim: RHOT1 knockdown in human lung epithelial cells impaired PDGF secretion.
source: TFAM or RHOT1 knockdown in human lung epithelial cells impaired PDGF secretion from epithelial cells (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung epithelial cells in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PDGF secretion defect in RHOT1-knockdown human lung epithelial cells was rescued by introduction of mouse RHOT1.
source: This defect was rescued by introduction of mouse TFAM or RHOT1 (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from human lung epithelial cells in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RHOT1 knockdown in human lung fibroblasts compromised cell migration.
source: In addition, TFAM or RHOT1 knockdown in human lung fibroblasts compromised cell migration of fibroblasts (Figure 8G, Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data from human lung fibroblasts in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Migration defects in RHOT1-knockdown human lung fibroblasts were restored upon expression of mouse RHOT1.
source: Likewise, migration defects were restored upon expression of mouse TFAM or RHOT1 (Figure 8G, Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data from human lung fibroblasts in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mitochondria play a major role in conferring requisite cellular properties to both alveolar epithelial cells and myofibroblasts during alveologenesis.
source: We discovered a major role of mitochondria in conferring requisite cellular properties to both alveolar epithelial cells and myofibroblasts during alveologenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations throughout the study.

claim: Not all cellular processes are perturbed to the same extent when mitochondrial activity or distribution is perturbed.
source: We found that not all cellular processes are perturbed to the same extent when mitochondrial activity or distribution is perturbed.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on various developmental processes.

claim: While alveolar development is disrupted, saccule formation and cell-type specification are unaffected by mitochondrial perturbation.
source: For instance, while alveolar development is disrupted, saccule formation and cell-type specification are unaffected.
evidence: Observation from the phenotypic analysis of mutant mice.

claim: These observations highlight the differential requirement of mitochondrial function in a given cellular process.
source: These observations highlight the differential requirement of mitochondrial function in a given cellular process.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effects of mitochondrial dysfunction on different processes.

claim: Events that necessitate a higher demand for energy will be the first to exhibit phenotypes once mitochondrial function is compromised.
source: Events that necessitate a higher demand for energy will be the first to exhibit phenotypes once mitochondrial function is compromised.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed differential sensitivity to mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: The severity of phenotypes resulting from a reduction in mitochondrial function could be used to characterize the energy demand for a particular cellular process in development.
source: It implies that the severity of phenotypes resulting from a reduction in mitochondrial function could be used to characterize the energy demand for a particular cellular process in development.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the utility of mitochondrial perturbation studies.

claim: Secretion of the PDGF ligand from alveolar epithelial cells is impaired due to mitochondrial dysfunction in either activity or distribution.
source: Secretion of the PDGF ligand from alveolar epithelial cells is impaired due to mitochondrial dysfunction in either activity or distribution.
evidence: Inferred from the PDGF secretion assay results.

claim: The actomyosin cytoskeleton likely underlies the defect in PDGF secretion.
source: We surmise that the actomyosin cytoskeleton likely underlies this defect.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the known role of the cytoskeleton in vesicular transport.

claim: The energy produced by mitochondria is required in many key steps of vesicular transport and membrane fusion.
source: However, it is also possible that the energy produced by mitochondria is required in many key steps of vesicular transport and membrane fusion.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Failure to power the actomyosin cytoskeleton in myofibroblasts due to disruption of mitochondrial activity or distribution could cause the contraction and/or migratory defect.
source: Similarly, failure to power the actomyosin cytoskeleton in myofibroblasts due to disruption of mitochondrial activity or distribution could cause the contraction and/or migratory defect.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the known role of the cytoskeleton in cell migration.

claim: ATP produced by mitochondria is known for the assembly of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: ATP produced by mitochondria is known for the assembly of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about ATP and cytoskeleton assembly.

claim: mTOR complex 1 is a key player in controlling mitochondrial function during alveolar formation.
source: Our work shows that mTOR complex 1 is a key player in controlling mitochondrial function during alveolar formation.
evidence: Inferred from the alveolar defects and reduced mitochondrial function in Rptor-deficient lungs.

claim: This is consistent with the role of mTORC1 in regulating mitochondrial function in cell-based assays.
source: This is consistent with the role of mTORC1 in regulating mitochondrial function in cell-based assays.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about mTORC1 function.

claim: Changes in cellular properties due to disturbed mitochondrial activity and distribution contribute to the pathogenesis of COPD/emphysema.
source: We speculate that changes in cellular properties due to disturbed mitochondrial activity and distribution contribute to the pathogenesis of COPD/emphysema (Ryter et al., 2018; Caldeira et al., 2021; Hara et al., 2018; Cloonan and Choi, 2016).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the findings in human emphysema samples and cited literature.

claim: Disturbance of mitochondrial function and cellular properties could be related to inflammatory responses in COPD/emphysema.
source: Disturbance of mitochondrial function and cellular properties could be related to inflammatory responses in COPD/emphysema.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about disease mechanisms.

claim: Energy production by mitochondria is channeled in a spatially specific manner to power cellular machinery and drive cellular processes in distinct cell types.
source: In particular, energy production by mitochondria is channeled in a spatially specific manner to power cellular machinery and drive cellular processes in distinct cell types.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of localized mitochondrial distribution and function.

claim: Diverse cell types and cellular processes have a unique energy demand, which is likely executed by a signaling network.
source: Diverse cell types and cellular processes have a unique energy demand, which is likely executed by a signaling network.
evidence: Inferred from the differential sensitivity of various processes to mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: Alveolar formation requires coordinated movement and interaction between alveolar epithelial cells, mesenchymal myofibroblasts, and endothelial cells/pericytes to produce secondary septa.
source: Alveolar formation requires coordinated movement and interaction between alveolar epithelial cells, mesenchymal myofibroblasts, and endothelial cells/pericytes to produce secondary septa.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about alveolar formation.

claim: These processes rely on the acquisition of distinct cellular properties to enable ligand secretion for cell-cell signaling and initiate morphogenesis through cellular contraction, cell migration, and cell shape change.
source: These processes rely on the acquisition of distinct cellular properties to enable ligand secretion for cell-cell signaling and initiate morphogenesis through cellular contraction, cell migration, and cell shape change.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about cellular processes in development.

claim: Mitochondrial activity and distribution play a key role in bestowing cellular functions on both alveolar epithelial cells and mesenchymal myofibroblasts for generating secondary septa to form alveoli in mice.
source: In this study, we showed that mitochondrial activity and distribution play a key role in bestowing cellular functions on both alveolar epithelial cells and mesenchymal myofibroblasts for generating secondary septa to form alveoli in mice.
evidence: Summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Mitochondrial function is tightly regulated to empower cellular machineries in a spatially specific manner.
source: These results suggest that mitochondrial function is tightly regulated to empower cellular machineries in a spatially specific manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of localized mitochondrial distribution and function.

claim: Regulation via mitochondria is required for secretion of ligands, such as platelet-derived growth factor, from alveolar epithelial cells to influence myofibroblast proliferation and contraction/migration.
source: Indeed, such regulation via mitochondria is required for secretion of ligands, such as platelet-derived growth factor, from alveolar epithelial cells to influence myofibroblast proliferation and contraction/migration.
evidence: Inferred from the PDGF secretion and signaling defects observed in mitochondrial mutants.

claim: Mitochondrial function enables myofibroblast contraction/migration during alveolar formation.
source: Moreover, mitochondrial function enables myofibroblast contraction/migration during alveolar formation.
evidence: Inferred from the migration defects observed in mitochondrial mutants.

claim: These findings yield novel mechanistic insights into how mitochondria regulate pivotal steps of alveologenesis.
source: Together, these findings yield novel mechanistic insights into how mitochondria regulate pivotal steps of alveologenesis.
evidence: Summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: These findings highlight selective utilization of energy in cells and diverse energy demands in different cellular processes during development.
source: They highlight selective utilization of energy in cells and diverse energy demands in different cellular processes during development.
evidence: Inferred from the differential sensitivity of various processes to mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: This work serves as a paradigm for studying how mitochondria control tissue patterning.
source: Our work serves as a paradigm for studying how mitochondria control tissue patterning.
evidence: Statement about the broader significance of the work.

claim: Defective alveologenesis underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD).
source: Defective alveologenesis underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Silva et al., 2015), and ongoing destruction of alveoli is characteristic of chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) (Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Silva et al., 2015.

claim: Ongoing destruction of alveoli is characteristic of chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD).
source: Defective alveologenesis underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Silva et al., 2015), and ongoing destruction of alveoli is characteristic of chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) (Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Patel et al., 2019.

claim: COPD is a major cause of morbidity and mortality globally.
source: COPD is a major cause of morbidity and mortality globally (Barnes et al., 2015; Rodríguez-Castillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Barnes et al., 2015 and Rodríguez-Castillo et al., 2018.

claim: During alveolar formation, alveolar epithelial cells, myofibroblasts, and endothelial cells/pericytes undergo coordinated morphogenetic movement to generate secondary septa within saccules.
source: During alveolar formation, alveolar epithelial cells (type I [AT1] and type II [AT2] cells), myofibroblasts, and endothelial cells/pericytes undergo coordinated morphogenetic movement to generate secondary septa within saccules.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about alveolar formation.

claim: Secondary septa are comprised of a layer of alveolar epithelial cells that ensheathes a core of myofibroblasts and endothelial cells/pericytes.
source: As a result, secondary septa are comprised of a layer of alveolar epithelial cells that ensheathes a core of myofibroblasts and endothelial cells/pericytes.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about secondary septa structure.

claim: Secondary septa formation (or secondary septation) is the most important step during alveolar formation.
source: Secondary septa formation (or secondary septation) is the most important step during alveolar formation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about alveolar development.

claim: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) produced by alveolar epithelial cells is a key player in controlling myofibroblast proliferation and contraction/migration during alveologenesis.
source: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) produced by alveolar epithelial cells is a key player in controlling myofibroblast proliferation and contraction/migration during alveologenesis (Boström et al., 1996; Lindahl et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Boström et al., 1996 and Lindahl et al., 1997.

claim: In response to PDGF signaling, the traditional model posits that myofibroblasts proliferate and migrate to the prospective site of secondary septation and secrete elastin.
source: In response to PDGF signaling, the traditional model posits that myofibroblasts proliferate and migrate to the prospective site of secondary septation and secrete elastin.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the traditional model of alveolar formation.

claim: Myofibroblasts and endothelial cells/pericytes are subsequently incorporated with alveolar epithelial cells to form secondary septa.
source: Myofibroblasts and endothelial cells/pericytes are subsequently incorporated with alveolar epithelial cells to form secondary septa.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about secondary septa formation.

claim: All of these principal components play a key role in driving secondary septa formation.
source: All of these principal components play a key role in driving secondary septa formation (Chao et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Chao et al., 2016.

claim: Generation of alveoli increases the surface area and efficiency of gas exchange, enabling high activity in terrestrial environments.
source: Generation of alveoli increases the surface area and efficiency of gas exchange, enabling high activity in terrestrial environments.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about alveolar function.

claim: Mitochondrial activity is essential for every biological process.
source: Mitochondrial activity is essential for every biological process, and mitochondria provide a major source of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Labbé et al., 2014; Chan, 2020).
evidence: Cited from Labbé et al., 2014 and Chan, 2020.

claim: Mitochondria provide a major source of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: Mitochondrial activity is essential for every biological process, and mitochondria provide a major source of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Labbé et al., 2014; Chan, 2020).
evidence: Cited from Labbé et al., 2014 and Chan, 2020.

claim: We have limited mechanistic insight into how mitochondria control cellular processes in vivo.
source: Unexpectedly, we have limited mechanistic insight into how mitochondria control cellular processes in vivo.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Little is known about whether certain cellular processes have a higher energy demand during alveolar formation.
source: In particular, little is known about whether certain cellular processes have a higher energy demand during alveolar formation.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Mitochondria exhibit dynamic distribution within individual cells.
source: Mitochondria exhibit dynamic distribution within individual cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Mitochondrial distribution is mediated by the cytoskeletal elements that include microtubules, F-actin and intermediate filaments.
source: This process is mediated by the cytoskeletal elements that include microtubules, F-actin and intermediate filaments.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial transport mechanisms.

claim: Rhot1 (ras homolog family member 1), also called Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase 1), encodes an atypical Ras GTPase and plays an essential role in mitochondrial transport.
source: For instance, Rhot1 (ras homolog family member 1), which is also called Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase 1), encodes an atypical Ras GTPase and plays an essential role in mitochondrial transport (Devine et al., 2016).

claim: RHOT1 associates with the Milton adaptor (TRAK1/2) and motor proteins (kinesin and dynein), and tethers the adaptor/motor complex to mitochondria.
source: RHOT1 associates with the Milton adaptor (TRAK1/2) and motor proteins (kinesin and dynein), and tethers the adaptor/motor complex to mitochondria.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about RHOT1 function.

claim: This machinery facilitates transport of mitochondria via microtubules within mammalian cells.
source: This machinery facilitates transport of mitochondria via microtubules within mammalian cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial transport.
